title: Alive or Not? — Parent Guide
endLine: No single clue decides life; check the whole list together.

scenes.tts: A toy car moves. A dry bean sits still. Which one is alive? Use this twenty-five-minute sort to help your child practice looking closely. They make a rule and check it against what they find.
scenes.caption: A toy car moves. A dry bean sits still. Which one is alive? Use this twenty-five-minute sort to help your child practice looking closely. They make a rule and check it against what they find.
scenes.visual: Friendly schematic top-down drawing of a warm wooden kitchen table filling the frame. Two big oval sorting mats sit side by side, labeled Alive and Not alive. A red toy car rolls smoothly onto the Alive mat while a large cream-colored lima bean hops onto the Not alive mat. A small question mark pulses gently between them. No photos of real children.
scenes.narration: A toy car moves. A dry bean sits still. Which one is alive? Use this twenty-five-minute sort to help your child practice looking closely. They make a rule and check it against what they find.

scenes.visual: The same kitchen table stays in view as the mats slide slightly down and a clean, high-contrast banner unfolds across the top: Alive or Not? — Parent Guide. Subtle ambient drift on the table objects keeps the frame alive.

scenes.tts: Fill a basket with ten to twelve household things. Start with a houseplant, an apple, a dry leaf, a stick, and a shell. Add a rock, a spoon, and a toy car. Set out paper and a pencil. Use one or two large dry kitchen beans. Skip garden-shop seed packets.
scenes.caption: Fill a basket with ten to twelve household things. Start with a houseplant, an apple, a dry leaf, a stick, and a shell. Add a rock, a spoon, and a toy car. Set out paper and a pencil. Use one or two large dry kitchen beans. Skip garden-shop seed packets.
scenes.visual: Same kitchen table. A woven basket sits on the left, filling 60 percent of frame height. As each item is named, simple friendly schematic drawings glide into the basket one by one: potted houseplant, red apple, dry brown leaf, twig, smooth shell, gray rock, silver spoon, toy car, and two large lima beans. A tiny red X gently crosses out a garden seed packet to the side before it fades.
scenes.narration: Fill a basket with ten to twelve household things. Start with a houseplant, an apple, a dry leaf, a stick, and a shell. Add a rock, a spoon, and a toy car. Set out paper and a pencil. Use one or two large dry kitchen beans. Skip garden-shop seed packets.

scenes.tts: First, ask your child to sort everything into two piles, alive and not alive. Hold back from correcting them. Instead, ask, how did you decide, and write down their rule in their own words. Listening first lets your child test their own idea.
scenes.caption: First, ask your child to sort everything into two piles, alive and not alive. Hold back from correcting them. Instead, ask, how did you decide, and write down their rule in their own words. Listening first lets your child test their own idea.
scenes.visual: The basket tips gently as items glide onto the two tabletop mats, Alive and Not alive, with the toy car sitting in Alive and the lima bean in Not alive. A clean notepad slides in at the bottom right; a schematic pencil writes the short label: My rule. Keep at most six visual elements active at once.
scenes.narration: First, ask your child to sort everything into two piles, alive and not alive. Hold back from correcting them. Instead, ask, how did you decide, and write down their rule in their own words. Listening first lets your child test their own idea.

scenes.tts: Compare the rock with a plant, a pet, or your child. Ask, what does it do that the rock does not? Write four clues together: grows, needs water, air and food, reacts, and makes more of its kind. Plants use light to make food. Check all four clues together.
scenes.caption: Compare the rock with a plant, a pet, or your child. Ask, what does it do that the rock does not? Write four clues together: grows, needs water, air and food, reacts, and makes more of its kind. Plants use light to make food. Check all four clues together.
scenes.visual: On the same table, the potted houseplant and the gray rock slide to the center, large and high-contrast. Beside them, a four-row schematic checklist card builds line by line as each clue is spoken, each row with a simple icon and bold label of three words or fewer: Grows, Water air food, Reacts, Makes more. The plant gently leans toward a sunbeam icon while the rock stays still.
scenes.narration: Compare the rock with a plant, a pet, or your child. Ask, what does it do that the rock does not? Write four clues together: grows, needs water, air and food, reacts, and makes more of its kind. Plants use light to make food. Check all four clues together.

scenes.tts: Try the checklist on the rock together first. Then let your child test each object and move it if their answer changes. With the car, ask, does it grow or make a baby car? A dry seed is still alive. Water and warmth let it sprout.
scenes.caption: Try the checklist on the rock together first. Then let your child test each object and move it if their answer changes. With the car, ask, does it grow or make a baby car? A dry seed is still alive. Water and warmth let it sprout.
scenes.visual: Keep the checklist on the right. Put the rock beside it and mark each clue it fails. Replace the rock with the toy car and show that movement alone leaves the other clues unmet. Then show the lima bean with a schematic thought bubble of water, warmth, and a sprout.
scenes.narration: Try the checklist on the rock together first. Then let your child test each object and move it if their answer changes. With the car, ask, does it grow or make a baby car? A dry seed is still alive. Water and warmth let it sprout.

scenes.tts: Now picture the dry leaf sitting on your table. If you are using just two piles, living and nonliving, pause and decide for yourself. Which pile does that dry leaf belong in, and why?
scenes.caption: Now picture the dry leaf sitting on your table. If you are using just two piles, living and nonliving, pause and decide for yourself. Which pile does that dry leaf belong in, and why?
scenes.visual: The checklist fades back slightly. The dry brown leaf rises large in the center of the table, hovering between two clear mats labeled Living and Nonliving. Above the leaf, a bold, readable question appears: Living or Nonliving?
scenes.narration: Now picture the dry leaf sitting on your table. If you are using just two piles, living and nonliving, pause and decide for yourself. Which pile does that dry leaf belong in, and why?

scenes.visual: Thinking pause. Keep the dry leaf gently drifting left and right above the Living and Nonliving mats with the question Living or Nonliving? still clearly visible on screen, plus a slow subtle progress bar along the bottom edge.

scenes.tts: For this sort, use Virginia’s kindergarten rule. The dry leaf goes in the living pile because it was part of a living plant. A rock goes in nonliving. For ages eight to ten, split the living pile into alive now and once alive.
scenes.caption: For this sort, use Virginia’s kindergarten rule. The dry leaf goes in the living pile because it was part of a living plant. A rock goes in nonliving. For ages eight to ten, split the living pile into alive now and once alive.
scenes.visual: The dry leaf settles smoothly onto the Living mat beside a faint schematic outline of a tree branch, showing where it came from, while the rock stays on Nonliving. Then the Living mat smoothly divides into two rings labeled Alive now and Once alive, with the houseplant and bean in Alive now and the dry leaf and stick gliding into Once alive.
scenes.narration: For this sort, use Virginia’s kindergarten rule. The dry leaf goes in the living pile because it was part of a living plant. A rock goes in nonliving. For ages eight to ten, split the living pile into alive now and once alive.

scenes.tts: Stay with your child throughout the activity. Keep all small objects, including large beans, away from children under four. Keep everything in the basket out of mouths. Count the beans back into a lidded jar yourself. If a child is choking or struggling to breathe, call nine one one.
scenes.caption: Stay with your child throughout the activity. Keep all small objects, including large beans, away from children under four. Keep everything in the basket out of mouths. Count the beans back into a lidded jar yourself. If a child is choking or struggling to breathe, call nine one one.
scenes.visual: Back to the kitchen table. The two lima beans lift cleanly into a schematic glass jar whose lid clicks shut, accompanied by a bold high-contrast badge: Under 4: no small items. A simple icon of the basket gets a clear No tasting label, followed by a clean red card reading: Choking? Call 911.
scenes.narration: Stay with your child throughout the activity. Keep all small objects, including large beans, away from children under four. Keep everything in the basket out of mouths. Count the beans back into a lidded jar yourself. If a child is choking or struggling to breathe, call nine one one.

scenes.tts: On your optional ten-minute walk, find three living and three nonliving things. Stay on a permitted path away from roads and water. Stay within arm’s reach near roads or water. Never leave your child alone near water of any depth. Look without picking. Wash hands with soap and water and check for ticks afterward.

Never leave your child alone near water of any depth. Look without picking. Wash hands with soap and water and check for ticks afterward.
scenes.visual: The table frame transitions smoothly to a friendly schematic park path with short grass, a distant pond separated by a clear dotted boundary, and a magnifying glass hovering over a tree and a rock (no hands picking). In the corner, a simple sink-and-soap icon bubbles gently for Wash hands.

scenes.tts: In this game, your child practices looking closely and stating a rule out loud. They test that rule against tricky objects and revise it when evidence pushes back. One clue alone can fool you, so checking every sign together is what counts.
scenes.caption: In this game, your child practices looking closely and stating a rule out loud. They test that rule against tricky objects and revise it when evidence pushes back. One clue alone can fool you, so checking every sign together is what counts.
scenes.visual: Return smoothly to the full sorted kitchen table: the houseplant, bean, and dry leaf sorted cleanly with the four-clue checklist glowing beside them. The schematic notepad updates from the first guess to a checked final rule as the four checklist icons light up together.
scenes.narration: In this game, your child practices looking closely and stating a rule out loud. They test that rule against tricky objects and revise it when evidence pushes back. One clue alone can fool you, so checking every sign together is what counts.
